What happens when 50 concurrent users attempt to book the exact same VIP shuttle seat at the exact same millisecond?
Double-booking? Frozen UI? Or a silent data race?
Most reservation systems look great in staging, but crumble under high-concurrency race conditions during peak flash sales.
In my latest architectural prototype, TransFlow AI — an executive intercity shuttle reservation platform for the Bandung – Jakarta corridor — I explored a resilient, production-grade architecture leveraging Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Optimistic UI rollback mechanisms, and action-oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
1️⃣ Optimistic UI with Instant Conflict Rollback:
Delivers instant 0ms perceived latency for passengers selecting seats. If a backend collision occurs (HTTP 409 Conflict), the UI immediately rolls back to its previous snapshot and gracefully marks the contested seat as held by another session—without breaking the user flow.
2️⃣ Anti-Race Distributed Atomic Lock:
Guarantees zero double-booking risk by securing seats through atomic locks with a 600-second (10-minute) TTL. Built-in stress test simulator executes 50 parallel bot threads competing for high-demand seats in real-time.
3️⃣ Action-Oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
The AI Concierge isn’t just a passive conversational bot. Through MCP tools, it acts as an autonomous operational copilot:
• Queries real-time tollway sensors (`get_corridor_telemetry`) to monitor weather radar and traffic bottlenecks along the Cipularang expressway.
• Dynamically calculates estimated arrival times (`calculate_dynamic_eta`).
• Grounded RAG with real physical constraints: The Toyota HiAce Premio stands at 2.28m, strictly barring it from entering the elevated MBZ tollway (2.10m clearance gantry)—enforcing routing through the lower expressway for structural safety.
4️⃣ Authentic Top-Down Automotive Blueprint:
A precision cabin blueprint reflecting Indonesian automotive ergonomics: Right-Hand Drive (RHD) cockpit, curbside electric sliding door, and a distinct separation between 100% Flat Floor seats (Rows 1 & 2) vs. Rear Wheel Well arch protrusions (Row 3).
🛠️ Tech Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Tailwind CSS, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Vector RAG, and jsPDF.

Over the past few months I've been building VenHub (Vendor Hub), an operations portal for vendors and internal teams at iForte Solusi Infotek. Field surveys and FTTH preventive maintenance used to run through many manual steps across several systems. VenHub moves that flow into one portal connected directly to Salesforce.

What VenHub does today: 
1. Connectivity Survey Salesforce sends surveys to vendors. Vendors fill in the Survey Form section by section, with photos per group. After submission, Salesforce creates or updates the Work Report and sends the status (Submitted, Approved or Rejected) back to VenHub.
2. Automatic PHS documents When a survey is Approved, the system calculates quantities against the PHS price list, generates the PDF, and uploads it to the Work Report in Salesforce. Failed deliveries retry automatically and can also be resent manually.
3. FTTH Preventive Maintenance Technicians submit a Customer ID, a category, and evidence photos. The photo count is validated against the category. Salesforce then sends the Work Order and Service Appointment status back.

What's next We plan to move more of the FTTH business process into VenHub, so vendors and internal teams work from one place.

Security and personal data protection VenHub holds customer and vendor data, so I built this in from the start, using Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP) as the reference:
1. Email OTP login, plus mandatory Microsoft Authenticator for Super Admins and Admins
2. Temporary account lock after repeated failed logins, and automatic logout when idle
3. Personal data masked in logs and in views for roles that shouldn't see it
4. Access to personal data recorded: who, which role, which endpoint
5. Automatic data retention for logs, histories and notifications

Tech stack:
1. Backend: Go (Gin), PostgreSQL, JWT, TOTP
2. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, Zustand, React Hook Form + Zod, acting as a BFF so the browser never handles the API token
3. Integrations: Salesforce (Apex/LWC and REST), internal email service
4. Deployment: Docker & Jenkins

What I learned:
1. Two-way integration needs retries, idempotency, and clear logs, or small failures are hard to trace.
2. Security and privacy cost far less when built in from the beginning.
3. As developers, we have to solve problems, keep learning, and adapt to whatever comes up. We shouldn't idolize a single platform, because a developer needs to see the big picture and pick the tools that will actually help the company.

Thanks to the team who helped along the way Andrey Sholinka, Dwiky Kurniawan, Daffa Asyqar Ahmad Khalisheka, Karina Virgi, Viriya Putta, Jessica Jetje Joanna.

posts.text:
Indonesia's AI opportunity is much bigger than chatbots.

Most of the conversation is about using AI. The bigger economic prize is building the industry behind it.
 
The scale is real. According to the e-Conomy SEA 2026 report by Google, Temasek and Bain, Indonesia's digital economy is projected to reach US$119 billion in GMV this year, up 16% year-on-year. The government has also cited an estimate that AI could contribute around US$366 billion to Indonesia's GDP by 2030.
 
These are projections, not guaranteed outcomes. And they raise a harder question:
 
How much of this value will Indonesian companies actually capture?
 
A large AI market does not automatically make us an AI industry. That requires capability across the value chain:
 
1. Infrastructure: data centres, GPU computing, sovereign cloud and reliable energy.
2. Platforms: local AI models, data engineering, MLOps and system integration.
3. Solutions: AI for banking, energy, manufacturing, healthcare and government.
4. Security & Governance: AI risk assessment, data protection, model security and continuous monitoring.
5. Talent: AI engineers, data scientists, cybersecurity and AI governance professionals.
 
Infrastructure attracts the headlines and the capital. The more durable opportunity lies in the capabilities to build, integrate, operate and secure the ecosystem.
 
The same report shows why. Indonesia has the largest generative AI user base in Southeast Asia, around 105 million people. Yet our depth of AI usage is the lowest among the SEA-6 markets.
 
We have the scale. The task now is to turn adoption into productivity, innovation and domestic value creation.
 
One layer deserves particular attention. AI without cybersecurity is an expensive experiment waiting for its first incident. As adoption accelerates, so do the risks: data exposure, model manipulation, identity abuse and AI-enabled attacks.
 
This is where ITSEC Asia aims to contribute: helping organisations adopt and secure AI responsibly, and developing cyber and AI talent through ITSEC Cyber & AI Academy.
 
The ambition should go beyond deploying someone else's technology. Indonesia should not only be the market for the AI revolution. We should be one of its builders.

Where should Indonesia focus first: AI infrastructure, local AI innovation, security, or talent?

[ What Does It Really Mean to Finish What You Start? ]

I have always liked the phrase "Finish What You Start" from Peter Hollins, particularly his perspective on the art of following through, taking action, execution, and self-discipline.

Without even realizing it, I have been applying this principle not only in my personal life but also in my professional journey. 

At Hilti Indonesia, we often talk about end-to-end applications and SPEC2SITE an integrated solution that connects design specifications directly to on-site installation, helping engineers and contractors deliver safer, faster, and more sustainable construction projects.

Let me explain why this matters.

During one of our visits to an Owner and Operator, we identified a challenge. They needed to perform vibration data collection, tribology, and alignment activities in several areas of their facility. However, some locations were not accessible with the existing arrangements, particularly at elevated positions. A new platform was therefore required.

This was where we started exploring how Hilti Group could contribute, particularly in developing the platform design and selecting the appropriate fastening anchors based on the platform loads and other relevant engineering requirements.

And this is where the SPEC2SITE and end-to-end application journey began.

We received the typical data and drawings, then used PROFIS Engineering to simulate the design, perform the calculations, prepare the engineering report, and provide recommendations for the appropriate anchor selection.

Once the engineering work was completed, we reviewed the design together with the contractor until it was accepted. Meanwhile, our Account Manager had already conducted the relevant tool demonstrations to prepare the installation team.

The process then moved to actual anchor installation by the contractor.

But we did not stop there.

To verify the installation workmanship, we also conducted on-site anchor testing using the HILTI HAT 180.

What amazed me most was seeing the entire process witnessed by the Owner and Operator to the Main Contractor and Subcontractor.

Why does this matter?

When engineering, design validation, product selection, installation preparation, execution, and on-site testing are connected, we are not simply delivering an anchor or a fastening solution. We are helping create confidence throughout the entire process.

For me, this is what end-to-end application really means. And perhaps this is how HILTI gives a different meaning to the philosophy I have always liked:

Don't just finish what you start. Finish it with excellence.

From the first engineering discussion to the final installation verification, every step matters. Because starting something is an intention. Following through is a commitment. And delivering it right is what makes the difference.

posts.text:
Every November 25, Indonesia celebrates National Teachers' Day with ceremonies, flowers, and speeches about "heroes without medals."

In 2024/2025, Indonesia had 3.06 million teachers. The student-teacher ratio was 15:1 in primary school, 14:1 in junior high, and 20:1 in senior high. That is better than many countries.

The problem in fact is distribution. In big cities, teachers pile up. In remote regions, one (1) teacher must teach three (3) subjects outside their field. Why? Because we force every school to teach 15-20 subjects per semester.

We built an impossible system, then blamed teachers for failing in it. The solution is not endless hiring. It is a slimmer curriculum and redistribution of the teachers we already have.

The 2026 education budget is IDR 769 trillion, 20% of state spending. But IDR 223.5 trillion goes to Free Nutritious Meals (MBG) program, the largest recipient. MBG may help nutrition, but it does not pay teachers, buy books, or fix a leaking roof.

The Constitutional Court has ruled: MBG is not education spending. It must be separated by 2028. Remove it, and the real education budget is only about IDR 545 trillion for 300,000 schools and 50 million students.

This explains the paradox: the budget rises, yet parents still pay. They pay for private school, pay "contributions" to public school, and in some places even pay to "buy a seat" in a good public school. People already paid taxes for education. They are forced to pay a second time because public money does not arrive.

Meanwhile, Indonesia scored 364 in math, 365 in reading, 389 in science. The OECD average is 463, 461, 482. Worse: 83% of 15-year-olds are below minimum competency in math, 73% in reading, 63% in science. Almost none reach the top levels.

Our children are not stupid. They are given an impossible curriculum, taught by exhausted teachers, in a system that rewards memorization over understanding.

Why has this never been fixed? Not because we don't know the cure, but because the disease benefits those who manage it. Publishers profit from many subjects. Bureaucracies profit from a big budget. Local leaders avoid moving teachers because it's politically costly.

Honoring teachers means three (3) reforms:
1. Slim the curriculum to 8-10 core subjects:
Focus on literacy, numeracy, science, language, and character. Teach few subjects deeply, not 20 subjects shallowly.

2. One teacher, one decent living:
End eternal honorary status. If the ratio is already 1:15, there's no excuse for a teacher working 40 hours to earn below minimum wage. Glory isn't a certificate on November 25. It's a salary on the first that allows dignity.

3. Separate MBG now and publish every rupiah:
Show per school where the money went and what it achieved. When money is visible, it's harder to waste.

Indonesia will be the world's 4th largest economy by 2050, with 288 million people and a median age of 31. That future needs a generation that can read critically and think independently.

🚀 Day 4/15 – First Complete Hibernate Program: Persisting Java Objects into MySQL | Java Backend Development Journey

Writing and executing an end-to-end database persistence workflow is where backend concepts truly come alive.

Today, I connected all the pieces from Day 3 and built my first complete Hibernate program to insert data into MySQL using modern Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate 6 standards.

📚 What I implemented and learned today:

✅ End-to-end application flow – Mapping a Java Student object through Hibernate (Session + Transaction + persist()) into MySQL (hibernate_db)
✅ Student Entity with Jakarta Persistence – Using @Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY), and @Column via jakarta.persistence
✅ XML mapping & configuration – Linking com.hibernate.entity.Student in hibernate.cfg.xml with hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=update
✅ Reusable SessionFactory (HibernateUtil) – Encapsulating SessionFactory initialization in a dedicated utility class for clean resource reuse
✅ Transaction lifecycle in Main – Managing openSession(), beginTransaction(), session.persist(), tx.commit(), and session.close()
✅ SQL output & database verification – Inspecting Hibernate-generated INSERT queries in Eclipse and verifying persisted records directly in MySQL
✅ persist() vs. save() – Adopting JPA-standard persist() (void return, recommended) over legacy save() (deprecated in Hibernate 6)
✅ Troubleshooting setup issues – Resolving Unknown database, Access denied, and No suitable driver errors

💡 My biggest takeaway:

Understanding the lifecycle of SessionFactory, Session, and Transaction—along with why modern Hibernate 6 favors JPA-standard persist() over deprecated methods—builds clean, maintainable backend habits from day one.
